original_question: A semi-dispersive billiard table is one whose boundary has dispersive inward-convex components together with neutral components such as line segments. Is every semi-dispersive billiard table hyperbolic?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 4: "Is every semi-dispersive billiard table hyperbolic?"
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's official formulation. It correctly identifies the class of tables as semi-dispersive, correctly highlights the mix of dispersive inward-convex pieces and neutral pieces, and asks exactly the right global question: whether every table in that class is hyperbolic.
missing_details: State the ambient setting explicitly: the paper is about planar billiards, i.e. compact connected billiard tables in R^2 with piecewise smooth boundary.
Specify what "hyperbolic" means in this paper: a billiard table is called hyperbolic when the corresponding billiard map is hyperbolic, not the flow or some other induced dynamics.

Anchor the term "semi-dispersive" to the paper's construction: starting from a not-necessarily-convex polygon, one replaces some but not all sides by smooth inward-convex arcs; the remaining sides are the neutral components.
Make clear that the paper then extends this terminology from circular arcs to general smooth inward-convex boundary curves, still within the planar piecewise-smooth setting.
Avoid wording that could broaden the problem beyond the paper: it is not asking about higher-dimensional billiards or billiards on arbitrary manifolds.
In the motivating polygonal model, line segments are not just an example of neutral components; they are the unreplaced sides of the polygon.
No ring/field, degree, homogeneity, nilpotency, or "for sufficiently large" quantifier issues arise here; the omitted assumptions are geometric and dynamical instead.
refined_question: Let Omega be a compact connected planar billiard table in R^2 with piecewise smooth boundary, in the class considered in Section 3: namely, Omega is semi-dispersive if it is obtained from a not-necessarily-convex polygon by replacing some but not all sides by smooth inward-convex arcs, so that the curved boundary pieces are dispersive components and the remaining boundary pieces are neutral components; more generally, the dispersive components may be any smooth curves convex inward. Must the associated billiard map of every such semi-dispersive billiard table be hyperbolic?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent formulation from Section 3 and Definition 2: does every semi-dispersive billiard table admit an invariant cone field for its billiard map?
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of the paper's official Problem 4 in Section 3, so the nearest faithful target is exactly that problem rather than a broader question about ergodicity, strict convexity, or polygonal billiards. The only paper-critical additions needed to make it stand alone are the planar piecewise-smooth setting from the introduction, the Section 3 meaning of hyperbolicity as hyperbolicity of the billiard map, and the precise Section 3 description of semi-dispersive tables via inward-convex dispersive components and neutral components. The reflection argument for one-neutral-component examples and the link to Problem 9 are supporting context, not part of the formal statement. The alternate formulation is justified because Section 3 explicitly says that hyperbolicity is equivalent to the existence of an invariant cone field.
